title: Water in Art
intro: Rivers carried trade and the dead, seas carried steamers and fishing fleets, and ponds held the reflections painters chased for decades. This walk follows water across nearly four thousand years, from a Nile boat model made for the afterlife to Monet's late lily pond. Along the way you will see water as a road, a blessing, a threat and, finally, a mirror.

stops.note: We begin on the Nile. This painted wooden model, with its oars, mast and crew of fifteen, was placed in an Egyptian tomb around 1875 BCE so its owner could keep travelling after death. For ancient Egyptians the river was the country's main highway, used for trade, government business and pilgrimage. Look at how the tiny rowers are arranged in neat rows along the hull: water here is not scenery but infrastructure, the thing that made daily life, and the next life, possible.

A hydria is a Greek water jar, the vessel women carried to and from the fountain house. This one, made around 350–330 BCE, is far too elegant for the daily walk to the well. Its ribbed body was formed in a mold and coated in glossy black, and a necklace was modeled on its neck in tiny pieces of gilded clay. It shows how something as ordinary as fetching water could be dressed up as a luxury object, fit for display or for the grave.

In the American Southwest, water was never taken for granted. On this Ancestral Pueblo jar, made between 950 and 1400, twin horned serpents stretch out from a central point. Such serpents were associated with the life-giving power of water across much of North America, and the stepped chevrons rising around them are widely linked to mountains, springs, rivers and gathering thunderstorms. Rather than picturing a river, the painter drew a sacred landscape and, in effect, a prayer for rain.

Soga Shōhaku painted this folding screen around 1761–62, and it turns water into drama. A dragon rises inside a mass of cloud, whipping up wind and rain, and the small boats below are caught in the turbulence while dark weather gathers around Mount Fuji. Ink and light colour are enough to convey spray, gusts and fear. Here water is no longer a road or a blessing; it is a force of nature with a mythical creature at its heart.

Aelbert Cuyp never travelled to Italy, yet he bathed this Dutch river view in a warm, southern-looking light. Painted around 1643–45, it shows a herdsman and cattle beside a slow, meandering river near Vianen. The flat land and wide water are typical of the Dutch countryside, where rivers shaped both the landscape and the economy. Notice the restrained, almost monochrome palette, a debt to Jan van Goyen, and how the calm surface of the water holds the whole scene together.

From Hiroshige's celebrated series One Hundred Views of Edo, this 1856 woodblock print shows the Sumida River at dusk, with the first stars appearing overhead. On the left leans the famous Pine of Success. In the corner, a roofed boat drifts with its green blinds lowered and a woman silhouetted behind them; two pairs of clogs in the prow hint that she is not alone. Water here is a stage for leisure and a little intrigue, the route to Edo's pleasure quarters.

Édouard Manet painted this calm sea in his Paris studio in 1864, working from sketches made on a family holiday at Boulogne-sur-Mer. It is one of his earliest seascapes. Look closely at the boats: they are brushed in quick, almost calligraphic strokes, yet each type is recognizable. A side-wheel steamer pushes up the Channel, leaving the slower sailing boats behind. It is a quiet picture about a noisy change, as steam began to overtake sail on modern waters.

In the 1870s Whistler began his Nocturnes, and this 1872 view of Southampton Water is one of the early examples. An inlet along the English Channel dissolves into the approaching night; shapes of ships and shore are barely there. Whistler believed painting could work like music, and his titles borrow from the concert hall. Instead of describing water, he uses it as an excuse to explore the tonal harmonies of darkness, a step toward abstraction that shocked many of his contemporaries.

We end at Giverny. During the First World War, after years of illness and grief, Claude Monet threw himself into a group of monumental water lily paintings, and alongside them he painted a suite of nineteen smaller canvases, including this one from 1917–19. There is no horizon and no shore, only lily pads, reflected sky and the shimmer of the surface. After a walk that began with water as a road, we finish with water as pure light and reflection.

title: Animals Through the Ages
intro: Animals have worked beside us, fed us, carried our prayers and stared back at us from the walls of palaces. This tour gathers donkeys, cats, horses, a giraffe, a sacred cow, a golden frog and a porcelain vulture, spanning more than four thousand years and five continents. Watch how each culture decided what an animal meant, and how artists found a way to show it.

stops.note: Our first animals are hard at work. This limestone fragment from an Egyptian tomb of about 2375 BCE shows donkeys being driven over harvested grain to separate wheat from chaff. The scene was a popular choice for tomb decoration, chosen from a set repertoire much as we might pick wallpaper. Look at the overlapping bodies and the rhythm of legs and ears: the carver turned a farming chore into a pattern, ensuring the tomb owner's fields would keep producing forever.

Cats were not just pets in ancient Egypt. This wooden coffin, made between 664 and 32 BCE, once held a mummified cat dedicated to a god in a temple. Animals were chosen for their connection to a particular deity, and the animal's soul was believed to carry messages between the human and divine worlds, asking for help with illness or wrongdoing. The upright, alert pose is a reminder that this creature was sent on an important errand.

Made in Greece around 750–730 BCE, close to the time of the first Olympic games, this small bronze horse was a gift for a god, probably left at a sanctuary. Horses were symbols of wealth, since only the affluent could keep them, so a horse offering said something about the giver too. The sculptor reduced the animal to a few simple shapes, long neck, slim legs, arched body, capturing its essence in the spare style favoured at the time.

A giraffe on a dining-room floor. This fifth-century Byzantine mosaic fragment once paved the home of a wealthy family in the eastern Mediterranean. Built from thousands of small stone cubes, it shows a handler leading a giraffe in front of a backdrop of scallop-shaped semicircles. Exotic animals, brought from Africa for spectacle and prestige, were a favourite subject for mosaic floors. Notice how the artist uses the giraffe's patches to show off control of colour and pattern.

Tenderness in sandstone. This Indian panel of about the ninth century shows a calf suckling from its mother, a Brahman cow identified by her hump, floppy ears, dewlap and upward-curving horns. In India cows enjoy a respected status and are regarded as nourishing mothers; even their dung is used for fuel and purification rituals. The sculptor gives the cow placid, half-closed eyes, a quiet image of care that still feels immediately familiar.

This cast-gold pendant, made by Coclé artists in what is now Panama between 500 and 1000, takes the form of a frog or toad. Across the ancient Americas the animal world was tied to social order. Frogs, connected with the start of the rainy season, were seen as summoners of water, and water meant crops. By wearing such an image, a ruler signalled responsibility for keeping the agricultural cycle turning. Look at the fine filigree, delicate as the creature itself.

Paulus Potter, who died young, made cows the heroes of Dutch painting. In this 1647 panel two cows and a young bull stand by a fence under a wide sky. Potter lavished attention on texture and colour of hide, bulky contours and characteristic poses, probably working from drawings made from life. The result borders on portraiture. In a country proud of its dairy farming, these animals were emblems of prosperity as well as nature.

Around 1728 Augustus, king of Poland and elector of Saxony, dreamed of recreating the animal kingdom in porcelain for a palace. The sculptor Johann Joachim Kändler, who drew this bird from life, modeled the vulture in 1734 at the Meissen manufactory. Porcelain was still an exclusive luxury in Europe, and a creature this large was a technical feat. The wrinkled head and ruffled feathers show how closely Kändler observed his subject.

We end with Franz Marc, the German Expressionist who wanted to paint the world as animals might feel it. The Bewitched Mill, from 1913, followed a stay in Merano, Italy. On the left sit the houses and mill of human life; on the right, trees and animals fill a lyrical, brightly coloured zone. Marc called the harmony he sensed between the two magical. After thousands of years of animals as workers, offerings and status symbols, here they are companions in a shared world.

title: Faces: Portraits Across the Millennia
intro: Why make a likeness of someone? To house a soul, to project power, to remember a friend, or simply to see yourself clearly. This tour moves from an Egyptian official carved in granite more than 3,500 years ago to Modigliani's newlyweds of 1916. Look at each face in turn and ask what the artist wanted us to notice and what they chose to leave out.

stops.note: This granite head of an official, made in Egypt around 1773–1650 BCE, once belonged to a full statue probably displayed in a tomb chapel. Note the striped wig tucked neatly behind his ears. Such statues were not simply memorials: they were receptacles for the ka, or soul. Priests performed the Opening of the Mouth ceremony so that the person could breathe, eat, hear and see in the afterlife. This portrait's job was to keep someone alive.

Earlier Roman emperors were clean-shaven. Hadrian, who reigned from 117 to 138 CE, wore a beard, perhaps in emulation of the Greek philosophers he admired, and set a fashion. In this marble portrait the neat beard contrasts with thick curls around the face. Look at the eyes: the sculptor carved the irises and pupils instead of painting them on, a new trend in Roman portraiture. Across the empire, images like this made the emperor's face instantly recognizable.

Painted portraits rarely survive from antiquity, but Egypt's dry climate preserved this one. Made in the second century, when Egypt was under Roman rule, it was painted in encaustic, pigment mixed with wax, on linden wood and placed over the face of a mummy. The heavy-lidded eyes, narrow chin and full lips capture an individual, while his curly hair and trimmed beard follow Roman fashion. The ivy wreath and gold add a festive note to a funerary image.

On the other side of the world, the Moche of Peru's north coast made ceramic vessels like this one between about 600 and 700. They are the only clear examples of portraiture, in the Euro-American sense, from the ancient Andes. Look at the individual features and the headdress. These vessels were often placed in burials, and they may also have been sent to other elite households as emblems of authority, standing in for the person they depict.

Rogier van der Weyden painted Jean Gros, an administrator to the future duke of Burgundy, around 1460–64. The panel was once half of a diptych: Gros's prayerful gaze was directed toward an image of the Virgin and Child on the other wing. His coat of arms, motto and initials on the back identify him. This is a portrait built for devotion and status at once, rendered with the crisp detail that made Netherlandish oil painting famous.

Rembrandt was twenty-five when he painted this in 1631, and it is not really a commissioned portrait. It is a character study, a type he loved, using a favourite model, once thought to be his father, dressed from the artist's collection of costumes. The gold chain and steel gorget suggest an honoured military career; the plumed beret belongs to an earlier age. Watch how light falls across the weathered face while everything else sinks into shadow.

Van Gogh painted more than 35 self-portraits, and this one dates from 1887, when he was living in Paris and absorbing the lessons of Seurat and pointillism. Instead of smooth modeling, the face is built from intense dabs of colour that seem to vibrate around the steady eyes. It is a portrait of a painter looking hard at himself, and it feels less like a likeness than a record of energy and presence.

This wooden figure represents Metang, tenth king of Batufam in the Cameroon Grassfields, carved around 1912–14 by the eastern Bangwa artist Mbeudjang. Although called a portrait, it was never meant to be lifelike. Commemorative figures like this are idealized images of kingship, and they served as partners to rulers in protecting the realm and its people. Set it beside the Egyptian official at the start of the tour: both are portraits with work to do.

Our final faces belong to a couple. The sculptor Jacques Lipchitz commissioned this double portrait from his friend Amedeo Modigliani in 1916, to mark his marriage to the poet Berthe Kitrosser, and partly to help the struggling painter financially. Modigliani's elongated forms and almond eyes are unmistakable, yet the pose, his hand on her shoulder, feels personal. After emperors, kings and souls in need of a home, we end with a portrait made out of friendship.

title: Gods and Heroes
intro: Every culture tells stories about powers greater than ourselves: gods who rule the dead, goddesses who make the corn grow, heroes who fight monsters. This tour travels from Egypt and Greece to India, China, the Maya world and the Aztec capital, then into Christian Europe. The stories differ, but you will notice the same big themes returning again and again: death and rebirth, harvest, and the struggle of order against chaos.

stops.note: Osiris was the ruler of the underworld and, in Egyptian myth, the country's first king. This finely cast copper-alloy statuette, made between 664 and 332 BCE, shows him in mummified form holding a shepherd's crook and flail, symbols of royal authority. Egyptians bought figures like this from temple workshops and left them in shrines to give thanks for answered prayers or to ask for health and long life. Osiris, who died and lived again, promised renewal.

Athena was the patron goddess of Athens, and her helmeted profile was stamped on the city's silver coins. While other cities updated their designs, Athens kept this image for centuries to signal that its money could be trusted, and Athenian coinage became a standard across the Mediterranean. Hold this small coin in your mind's eye as a pocket-sized shrine: a goddess who circulated through markets far beyond her temple.

One of the great Greek myths of loss and return, carved on a Roman sarcophagus around 190–200 CE. Read the panel from left to right: Demeter, goddess of the harvest, drives her chariot in search of her daughter; Persephone kneels at the centre, looking up; on the right, Hades carries her off to the underworld. The myth explained the seasons, as Persephone spends part of each year below ground, and it offered hope to mourners that death might not be final.

These earthenware panels once fitted beneath the pitched roof of a Han dynasty tomb in first-century China. Winged figures ride dragons over hills or waves. In Han belief such beings were immortals, xian, and placing them in a tomb expressed the hope that the soul of the dead could leave the earthly world, rise to heaven and become immortal too. Look at the sense of speed in the dragons' bodies; this is a journey, not a portrait.

Considered one of the most sublime images in Indian art, the dancing Shiva, Nataraja, was cast in bronze during the Chola period, around the tenth or eleventh century. Shiva's cosmic dance sets the rhythm of life and death in motion, destroying the world so that creation can begin again. His right leg is planted on a demon representing ignorance. Walk around the figure in your imagination: the limbs radiate outward like a wheel in constant motion.

This vessel was painted in the late 700s by Aj Maxam, a royal artist of the Naranjo kingdom in Guatemala, whose name we know. It shows a Maya ruler dressed as the maize god, a deity bound up with death and resurrection, as the soul of the deceased is accompanied into the realm of the dead. Like maize, which sprouts again each year, the soul would be reborn. Compare it with Osiris and Persephone: a different continent, a similar hope.

Xilonen was the Aztec goddess of young maize, a youthful figure of fertility and renewal. In this basalt head, made between 1400 and 1500, two large ears of corn rise from her headband and their tassels flow down her back. The Mexica held a July festival in her honour to celebrate the first fruits of summer, when a young girl impersonated the goddess and danced to bring an abundant harvest. Stone here holds the memory of a living ritual.

Heroes need monsters. Painted in Catalonia in 1434–35 by Bernat Martorell, this panel shows Saint George, the model Christian knight, who in the legend saves a town and rescues a princess by slaying a dragon. Look at the halo, the armour and the scaly beast: all are built up in raised stucco, catching the light. The story of order defeating chaos is as old as myth itself, and here it is retold with late Gothic splendour.

We end on Mount Olympus. Around 1608 the Dutch painter Joachim Wtewael painted the Greek gods defeating the giants, an ancient race that challenged their rule. Painted on copper, the small picture glows almost like a jewel, and its twisting, athletic bodies and dramatic contrasts of light show off the Mannerist style fashionable around 1600. Two thousand years after Athena's coins, the old gods were still a favourite way to stage the struggle between order and chaos.

title: Blue
intro: Blue was once among the hardest colours to make and the most expensive to buy, so it was saved for jewellery, sacred garments and the skies of heaven. This colour walk follows blue through glass, faience, glaze, pastel and paint, from ancient Egypt to Munch's Norway. Let your eye lead the way, and notice how the same colour can feel precious, holy, fashionable or unsettling.

stops.note: Blue glass, bent into a ring. This earring was made in Egypt around 1400–1295 BCE by heating blue glass, wrapping it around a rod and fusing it with a twisted cane of white and black. During the New Kingdom men, women and children of all classes wore earrings, and a wire through the top once passed through the wearer's ear. Glassmaking was a prized skill, and blue, the colour of the sky and the Nile, made even a small ornament feel special.

This net of blue faience beads, made in Egypt in the 600s BCE, was laid over a mummified body. At its centre is a scarab, the dung beetle that represented Khepri, the sun god at dawn. As the sun was born anew each morning, Egyptians hoped to be reborn after death. Blue faience, a glazed ceramic that imitated precious stones like turquoise and lapis lazuli, wrapped the dead in the colour of sky and renewal.

In late fifteenth-century Italy, Venetian glassblowers specialized in brilliant blue glass meant to imitate sapphires. This footed bowl of about 1490 is a luxury statement: its enamelled decoration of cherubs and fantastical sphinxes, and its classical shape, show the Renaissance passion for ancient Rome. Hold it up to an imagined window and the blue would glow. Here blue is less about heaven than about wealth, taste and craftsmanship.

Iznik potters in Ottoman Turkey first took their cue from blue-and-white Chinese porcelain, but by the late sixteenth century, when this dish was made, they had created a style of their own. Underglaze blue and turquoise sit beside red and black on a white ground. A fish-scale pattern fills the background, and two sweeping saz leaves, named for the reed pen used in drawing, arc across it. Blue here is lively and decorative, a colour for the dining table.

The centrepiece of El Greco's first major Spanish commission, painted in 1577–79. The Virgin rises on a crescent moon, a symbol of her purity, while the apostles below react with amazement. For centuries, the Virgin's robes were painted in costly blue, and El Greco uses broad strokes of it to lift the eye upward toward heaven. His bold colour made this painting a favourite of later artists, including Pablo Picasso and Mary Cassatt.

Rosalba Carriera, one of the originators of the Rococo style, drew this sitter around 1730 in pastel on blue paper. The paper's tone shows through, cooling the shadows and setting off the powdery pinks of skin and the bright parrot. The model may have been a young Englishwoman, perhaps a daughter of Lord Manchester. Notice how blue here works quietly, as a ground that makes every other colour sing, and helps create the picture's grace and charm.

Gustave Caillebotte's masterpiece of 1877 is a symphony of blue-grey. Rain has slicked the cobblestones of a newly built Paris intersection, and fashionable pedestrians shelter under recently invented umbrellas. The wet, cool tones unify the whole scene, from the pavement to the sky to the dark coats. It is blue as the colour of modern city weather, and a painting you almost feel you could walk into.

Painted in 1893, the same year as The Scream, Edvard Munch's The Girl by the Window is steeped in deep blue. A girl in a nightgown looks out from a darkened room at the city beyond; the floor tilts steeply and shadows swallow almost everything else. Here blue is no longer precious or holy. It is the colour of night, solitude and unease, and it shows how the same hue can completely change its mood.

We finish in London. Monet painted the Houses of Parliament from a terrace at St Thomas' Hospital, in the afternoon and at sunset, around 1900–01. The building dissolves into mist, rendered in blues and violets that make stone look like vapour. Monet was inspired by Whistler's paintings of the Thames, and the choice of viewpoint recalls Turner too. After thousands of years as a precious material, blue has become the colour of air itself.

title: A Walk Through Impressionism
intro: The classic tour, in chronological order. Starting with the coastal painter who taught Monet to see, it follows the Impressionists from Normandy beaches to Parisian railway stations, millinery shops and nurseries, then on to the series paintings and the water lilies of Monet's old age. Along the way, look for the movement's big ideas: painting outdoors, modern subjects, broken brushwork and the fleeting effects of light.

stops.note: Before Impressionism had a name, there was Johan Barthold Jongkind. His Entrance to the Port of Honfleur, painted in 1863–64, shows the kind of coastal scene that fascinated the younger painters. Monet later claimed that it was Jongkind who educated his eye. Though Jongkind finished his canvases in the studio, he worked hard to keep the freshness of his outdoor sketches. Look at the loose sky and lively water: the seeds of a revolution are already here.

In 1867 the young Claude Monet was staying with his aunt at Sainte-Adresse, near Le Havre, where he grew up. He began this beach scene outdoors and probably revised it in the studio. Technical study has shown that it started as a picture of yachts and tourists but became a view of sailboats and local fishermen. The broad strokes of sand and cloud, and the cool light, show Monet working out how to paint what he saw directly.

Berthe Morisot was a founding member of the Impressionist group, and this painting of 1875–80 shows why she was admired. A woman adjusts her hair at a mirror, a subject many male artists painted, but Morisot's view is intimate rather than voyeuristic. The feathery strokes of lavender, pink, blue, white and grey are pure Impressionism. She signed her name along the bottom of the mirror, as if the whole image were as fleeting as a reflection.

The Impressionists loved modern Paris, and nothing was more modern than the railway. Monet made twelve paintings of the Gare Saint-Lazare, and in this one from 1877 a train from Normandy arrives beneath the glass-and-iron shed. What interested him was the mix of artificial and natural effects: clouds of steam trapped under the roof and daylight streaming through the glass. The subject is industrial, but the real theme is atmosphere.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir painted Two Sisters (On the Terrace) in 1881. Despite the title, the girls were not related. The older one gazes past her companion, whose flushed cheeks suggest she has just run into the picture. Behind them, a hazy riverside landscape dissolves into soft colour, and the basket of yarn in the foreground looks almost like a painter's palette. It captures Impressionism's gift for making a posed moment feel spontaneous and warm.

Degas preferred to call himself a realist, but he exhibited with the Impressionists throughout their group shows. In The Millinery Shop, worked on between 1879 and 1886, a milliner examines a hat. Hat-making was a respected trade, and Degas gives the woman a dress fine enough for an affluent customer. He playfully positions a hat with green trimmings so it seems to sit on her head. Notice the cropped, off-centre composition, a hallmark of his modern eye.

In 1890–91 Monet painted the stacks of wheat outside his house at Giverny again and again, working at several easels at once as the light changed, then refining the canvases in the studio. This one records a snowy, overcast day, with the stack snugly bedded down between bands of field and hill. The series marked a breakthrough in his career: the true subject is no longer the haystack but the weather and the hour.

Mary Cassatt was the only American invited to exhibit with the original French Impressionist group. The Child's Bath, from 1893, is one of her masterworks. A mother washes her child's feet, and the viewpoint looks down on them from above. The bold patterns, strong outlines, cropped forms and flattened space come from Cassatt's study of Japanese woodblock prints. It shows how Impressionism, by the 1890s, was opening onto new ways of seeing.

The tour ends where Impressionism went furthest. During the First World War, after years of ill health and mourning, Monet began his monumental water lily paintings, and alongside them he made nineteen smaller canvases like this one of 1917–19. Horizon and shore vanish; there is only the pond's surface, flowers and reflected sky. More than fifty years after Sainte-Adresse, Monet had turned the pursuit of light into something close to abstraction.

title: Eat, Drink, Celebrate
intro: Pull up a chair. This tour is about the table: offerings for the dead, wine for the gods, tea for monks, chocolate kept under lock and key, and the noisy company of taverns from Haarlem to Long Island. Food and drink tell us who people were, what they valued and who was, or was not, invited to the feast.

stops.note: The first meal on our tour is one meant to last forever. This limestone relief of about 2050 BCE comes from an offering niche made for an Egyptian woman named Merettetiiyet. At the top, bearers bring offerings to sustain her in the afterlife; below, she faces visitors behind heaped piles of food. She holds a closed lotus, a flower that opens with the sun and sinks at night, a symbol of rebirth. Food here is nourishment for eternity.

Greeks rarely drank wine neat. They mixed it with water in jars like this stamnos, made around 450 BCE and painted by the artist known as the Chicago Painter. In red-figure style, the figures are left the natural colour of the clay. The scene shows women followers of Dionysos, the god of wine, a fitting subject for a vessel at the heart of a drinking party. Remarkably, this jar still has its original lid after nearly 2,500 years.

A drink can be a ritual. This twelfth-century Chinese tea bowl is Jian ware, dark stoneware with a lustrous glaze streaked in what is called hare's fur. Japanese monks treasured such bowls for tea-drinking rituals and called them temmoku, after a mountain monastery in south China. The conical shape fits neatly in cupped hands, and the dark glaze made the milky froth of whisked white tea look even brighter. Imagine the warmth of it.

Diego Velázquez painted this kitchen scene in Seville around 1618–20, when he was barely twenty. It is a bodegón, a Spanish pantry picture, and the pots, jugs and crumpled spice paper are rendered with astonishing care. At its centre is a young African woman at work. Slavery was widespread in Seville, and Velázquez's own family and teacher were enslavers; she may have been an enslaved servant. The painting reminds us to ask who prepared the feast.

The most famous party in Christian art. Giuseppe Maria Crespi painted The Wedding at Cana around 1686, the feast at which Jesus performed his first miracle. On the left Jesus speaks with his mother; on the right the astonished host and a servant taste the water he has turned into wine. Crespi fills the scene with luxurious details and small, personal exchanges, combining Venetian colour with the close observation of character loved in his native Bologna.

In Haarlem, Adriaen van Ostade built a long career painting peasant life, and tavern scenes were among his specialities. In Merrymakers in an Inn of 1674, villagers drink, talk and make music. Van Ostade used clear, fairly bright colours and fine brushwork to suit the taste of the later 1600s, and collectors loved the range of gestures and expressions in his jolly figures. Pick out one face and imagine the conversation.

Chocolate was a New World luxury. This tin-glazed earthenware jar, made in Puebla, Mexico, between 1725 and 1775, is Talavera poblana, a ceramic tradition in the town since the sixteenth century. Its owners probably added the locking metal lid to protect valuable contents such as cocoa beans, which were expensive at the time. The patterns show how local artisans adapted fashionable imported designs into something distinctly their own.

William Sidney Mount was among the first American artists to specialize in everyday life, and this 1835 painting shows a lively group of patrons in a country tavern. Look to the back corner, where an African American man stands apart. As a free Black man in 1830s New York he may have been able to enter the tavern, but he does not fully share in its community. The painting captures both conviviality and its limits.

We end with a sobering toast. While a patient at Saint-Rémy in 1890, Van Gogh often copied works by artists he admired, and The Drinkers is his vivid version of an image by Honoré Daumier. Van Gogh's colours are bright, yet there is real pathos in the men's concentration, as if they were trying to quench a thirst no drink could satisfy.
